title: SECTION A — PROFESSIONAL IDENTITY AND TITLES

questions.prompt: During a handover in front of Client Sam, Thr. Ada says, “Jane, Room 2 is ready — tell her to hurry.” Jane is the other therapist. What is the most professional repair, and why does first-name-only matter here?
options: Keep using first names. Clients enjoy seeing therapists as casual friends.
Address her as Therapist Jane or Thr. Jane. In front of clients, work-name-plus-title keeps a clear professional identity and shows the client a disciplined team, not a private chat.
Use a nickname so the client feels included in staff culture.
Say nothing; the client already knows who Jane is.

questions.prompt: A therapist is close friends with the Staff Manager after hours. On shift they refuse to use SM or SM + work name because “She’s my friend; titles are fake.” What is the Zura position?
options: Friendship cancels leadership titles during work.
Titles are only for people you do not like.
Familiarity does not remove professionalism. While she is carrying out SM responsibility, the role should be recognized. Knowing someone personally is not permission to erase the role.
Use the title only if other therapists are watching.

questions.prompt: After a correction, a therapist replies, “Okay o, Manager!” with a laugh and eye-roll. They later say, “I used the title, so it was respectful.” Was it?
options: Yes. Any use of a leadership word counts as respect.
No. Tone, facial expression, volume, and context can turn a title into mockery. A respectful word spoken sarcastically is still disrespect.
Yes, if the Manager is younger than the therapist.
Only wrong if a client heard it; among staff it is humour.

questions.prompt: A therapist shouts “YES SIR!” at a client who asked for lighter pressure, with an aggressive volume. They used an approved word. What failed?
options: Nothing. Sir is always enough.
The client should not request pressure changes.
The title must match the tone. Sir, Ma, or Madam can sound respectful or insulting depending on delivery. The word without respectful tone is not the standard.
Leaders may speak this way; therapists may not.

questions.prompt: A Lead Therapist asks to be called LT during assessments, not only “my guy.” A colleague ignores this because “We are all therapists.” What is being refused?
options: Unnecessary formality with no operational purpose.
A recognized leadership role that exists because responsibilities differ. Deliberately ignoring it because of friendship or sameness weakens coordination.
The colleague’s right to choose any name they like.
Proof that LT is superior as a human being.

title: SECTION B — CLIENTS: NAMES, DESCRIPTIONS AND DIRECT ADDRESS

questions.prompt: A therapist tells the next room, “The Indian man in Room 2 wants more oil,” even though the booking name is Client Raj. Why is this more than a small wording habit?
options: It is faster than using a name, so it is professional.
Where the name is known, use Client + name. Appearance, nationality, or body descriptions can become offensive, confuse the team, and teach others to identify people as objects rather than clients.
Nationality is the most accurate identifier.
It is allowed if the client cannot hear.

questions.prompt: Nobody asked the waiting guest’s name. Staff keep saying “that woman.” What should happen, and what does the name actually do?
options: Avoid asking; names create unwanted intimacy.
Politely ask, for example: “Please Sir/Ma, may I have your name?” Then use it. The name personalizes care, improves handovers, reduces physical descriptions, and helps the person feel recognized.
Guess a name so you do not have to ask.
Only reception may ever know names.

questions.prompt: A regular client says, “Just call me Babe, like last time.” What stays true even if they are familiar?
options: Repeated visits cancel professional address. Use pet names freely.

Familiarity does not automatically authorize pet names, romantic names, or sexualized names. Keep a respectful form (Mr./Ms./Sir/Ma/Madam or their professionally acceptable preference) unless there is an appropriate, professionally acceptable context.
The therapist should use Babe internally and Mr. only on paper.
Refuse all first names forever, even if they prefer a respectful first-name style.

questions.prompt: The client prefers “Ms. Grace” when spoken to. Internally, a therapist still says “that customer from yesterday.” Which pairing matches the standard?
options: Direct: any nickname. Internal: “the customer.”
Direct: Ms. Grace (or her known preference). Internal: Client Grace. Direct address and internal reference both stay respectful and specific.
Internal slang is fine if direct speech is polite.
Use Client Grace only in written reports, never speech.

questions.prompt: Two guests wait: one clearly wealthy, one not. A therapist uses “Sir” warmly with the first and “that guy” with the second. What standard is broken besides manners?
options: None. Important people deserve better titles.
Respect should not change because someone appears wealthy, influential, or important. Dignity is not a reward for status. Client + name and respectful direct address apply to both.
The second guest should be addressed only by room number.
Wealthy clients must be addressed as Manager.

title: SECTION C — COLLEAGUES, FRIENDSHIP AND WHAT CLIENTS HEAR

questions.prompt: Two friends shout each other’s first names aggressively across the corridor while a client is walking to the treatment room. They say it is “just how we talk.” What should they consider?
options: Clients never notice staff-to-staff talk.

Clients hear how therapists speak to each other. Aggressive shouting, mockery, or careless names can make the spa look poorly managed. Comfort with a friend is not permission to be careless with words at work.
Shouting is required so the whole floor knows who is needed.
Only English insults count; local-language jokes are always safe.

questions.prompt: A therapist uses a humiliating nickname for a colleague “as a joke.” The colleague laughs along. New staff copy it. What is the cultural risk?
options: Jokes never shape culture if people laugh.
New therapists learn culture by watching. If mockery is normalized, it spreads. Humiliating nicknames remain inconsistent with the standard even if the target pretends it is fine.
Copying proves the nickname is now official.
Only written nicknames are a problem.

questions.prompt: A therapist is angry after a missed towel. They call a junior “useless” in the linen room, then use “Thr. Tolu” politely in the meeting. What failed?
options: Nothing, because the meeting was professional.
Respect should be consistent, not a performance for important people. Position does not determine dignity. Junior staff deserve respectful address even during frustration.
Juniors should expect harsh names until they are senior.
Anger always authorizes any mode of address.

questions.prompt: A colleague needs help. Which request best matches professional colleague address without sounding cold?
options: “You, come here now.”
“Therapist Jane, please can you assist me?” Warmth can sit inside a professional form. The standard is not stiffness; it is identity plus courtesy.
No request is allowed until a leader speaks.
First name only, because “please” already shows respect.

questions.prompt: Staff form a clique: friends get first names and jokes; outsiders get clipped, cold titles used to freeze them out. Why is this still a mode-of-address problem?
options: Titles are only for outsiders; friends are exempt.
Different levels of respect based on friendship, seniority, or popularity create division. Professional forms should not become a weapon to include some people and exclude others.
Cliques improve teamwork.
Cold titles are always more professional than warmth.

title: SECTION D — LEADERSHIP, CORRECTION AND POWER

questions.prompt: A Supervisor uses their title while humiliating a therapist in front of others: “SP is talking — you will listen.” The words include a role. Is that the standard?
options: Yes. Leadership titles allow public humiliation.
No. Titles communicate responsibility, not greater human value. Leaders must demonstrate the same respect they expect. Humiliation is not professional address.
Yes, if the therapist made a real mistake.
Only Managers may humiliate; SPs may not.

questions.prompt: A therapist receives a fair correction and answers with insults. Another therapist gives the same correction by mocking the person’s work name. Who broke the standard?
options: Only the person who was corrected.
Both. Correction is not permission for disrespect in either direction: do not answer correction with insults, and do not correct by humiliating.
Neither, because correction is always harsh.
Only if a client was in the room.

questions.prompt: A therapist used the wrong work name once, accepted correction, and adjusted. Another repeatedly mocks the SM after being told to stop. How should accountability differ?
options: Punish both equally; any error is disciplinary.

Occasional forgetting plus accepting correction is normal adjustment. Repeated deliberate mocking of colleagues or leaders is a professional-conduct concern. The aim is a culture of intentional respect, not punishing harmless wording mistakes.
Ignore both; mode of address is meaningless.
Only written mistakes count.

questions.prompt: A Therapist Guide is correcting technique. A senior-tenured therapist says, “Don’t TG me; I was here first.” What has tenure been confused with?
options: Tenure always outranks a TG title on the floor.
Leadership roles exist for responsibility, not personal superiority. Professional address recognizes the role in that moment. Tenure is not a licence to erase the TG.
The TG should stop using any title with tenured staff.
The senior therapist should only be called Manager.

questions.prompt: Where private correction would work, a leader chooses a loud public dressing-down using the therapist’s name as a punchline. What should have guided them?
options: Public shame trains the whole team faster.
Correct privately and respectfully where that is appropriate. Using someone’s name to humiliate them is not “being firm.” Firmness without rudeness is still required.
Names should never be used during correction.
Only clients may be corrected privately.

title: SECTION E — CULTURE, CONSISTENCY AND THE FULL STANDARD

questions.prompt: A therapist says, “It’s only what I called her — she’s not actually hurt.” Why does Zura still treat repeated careless address as serious?
options: Because wording never affects culture.

How people address each other gradually forms culture. If careless talk is tolerated, it can grow into mockery, cliques, resistance to leadership, weak client boundaries, and hostility. Mode of address is part of order, professionalism, and dignity.
Because every slip must be a written warning.
Because titles exist only for legal documents.

questions.prompt: During handover, which script best shows identity, client dignity, and useful clinical detail together?
options: “The short guy likes it hard. Jane, go.”
“Therapist Clara, this is Client Sam. Client Sam prefers medium pressure and has tension around his shoulders.” Everyone is named with role; the client is not reduced to a body or a joke.
“Sam wants oil. The other one knows.”
Whisper the details so titles are unnecessary.

questions.prompt: A therapist uses perfect titles when the Manager is present and slang insults when they leave. What mindset is missing?
options: Titles are only a show for leadership.
“I can be comfortable without becoming careless.” Professional communication should be normal conduct, not a performance when someone important is watching.
The Manager should never see real staff culture.
Insults among peers build honesty.

questions.prompt: A colleague uses a sexually loaded nickname for another therapist “because we are close.” Why is this in a different category from forgetting “Thr.” once?
options: It is the same as a small title slip.
Degrading, discriminatory, or sexually inappropriate modes of address are a serious disciplinary concern. Closeness does not authorize sexualized naming at work.
Sexualized names are allowed if both people smile.
It is only a problem in client-facing rooms, not the staff area.

questions.prompt: Which sequence captures the Mode of Address Standard, and what must still sit on top of every title?
options: IGNORE ROLE → USE NICKNAME → SWITCH TONE WHEN ANGRY
IDENTIFY → ADDRESS → RESPECT → MAINTAIN. The word must match the tone. Warm without careless, familiar without disrespectful, friendly without inappropriate, firm without rude.
TITLE → FEAR → SILENCE
FRIENDSHIP FIRST → ROLE NEVER
